title: Local data at the singular points of an excellent normal surface
statement: Let $X$ be a normal integral Noetherian excellent scheme of dimension $2$ [def-pc-integral-scheme, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-exc-excellent-ring, def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring, def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Noetherian means that $X$ has a finite affine open cover by spectra of Noetherian rings; excellent means that the ring of every affine open is excellent. Then $X_{\rm reg}=\{x:\mathcal O_{X,x}\text{ is regular local}\}$ is open [def-weil-regular-scheme], and $X\setminus X_{\rm reg}$ is a finite set of closed points. For each of these points $x$, the ring $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is an excellent Noetherian normal local domain of dimension $2$, and its maximal-ideal-adic completion $\widehat A$ is a complete Noetherian normal local domain of dimension $2$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion].

source.place: Tags 07QT (definition-excellent, J-2), 07QU (lemma-finite-type-over-excellent, localization), 0C23 (lemma-completion-normal-local-ring), 07NV (lemma-completion-dimension); algebra.tex Tag 031S (lemma-criterion-normal, R1). The finite singular set is the normal-surface observation used in resolve.tex, Tag 0BGN.

proof.text: Choose the finite affine cover $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i$ in the Noetherian hypothesis. For $x\in U_i$ corresponding to $\mathfrak p$, the affine-stalk localization lemma identifies $\mathcal O_{X,x}= (R_i)_{\mathfrak p}$. These stalks are Noetherian by localization of a Noetherian ring. Since $X$ is normal, each of these stalks is a normal domain; hence every $R_i$ is a normal ring by the definition of normal ring. We use the same affine-stalk identification on any later affine neighbourhood.

source.place: Tag 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves), affine stalks; algebra.tex, localization of Noetherian rings and the definition of normal ring.

proof.text: For each $i$, excellence of $R_i$ includes J-2. Apply its defining condition to the identity finite type $R_i$-algebra $R_i$ (generated by the empty family). Thus the primes $\mathfrak p$ with $(R_i)_{\mathfrak p}$ regular local form an open subset of $U_i$. Step 1 identifies it with $X_{\rm reg}\cap U_i$. The union over the cover is $X_{\rm reg}$, which is consequently open. Put $Z=X\setminus X_{\rm reg}$; it is closed.

source.place: Tag 07QT (definition-excellent), J-2 applied to the identity algebra.

proof.text: For any affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq X$, one has $\dim R\leq2$. Indeed a prime chain of length $n$ gives, by the spectrum closed-subset dictionary, a strict reversed chain of irreducible closed sets $V(\mathfrak p)\subset W$. Taking their closures in $X$ preserves irreducibility and strictness: intersection of each closure with $W$ is the original closed set. The dimension definition therefore gives $n\leq\dim X=2$. Moreover the prime-localization bijection identifies prime chains in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ with chains of primes of $R$ contained in $\mathfrak p$. Since the affine-stalk localization lemma identifies $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with $R_{\mathfrak p}$ for $x\in W$ corresponding to $\mathfrak p$, every stalk has dimension at most two.

source.place: Tag 0055 (definition-Krull); algebra.tex Tags 00E3 (lemma-spec-localization) and the spectrum irreducible-closed-subset dictionary. Explicit prime-chain argument.

proof.text: Apply Serre's criterion to each Noetherian normal ring $R_i$ of Step 1. It has $(R_1)$, which says exactly that its prime localizations of dimension at most one are regular local. If $x\in Z\cap U_i$, its local ring is not regular, so its dimension is greater than one. By Step 3 its dimension is at most two. Hence $\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}=2$ for every $x\in Z$.

Every $x\in Z$ is closed in $X$. To see this, suppose $y\ne x$ is a specialization of $x$ and take an affine neighbourhood $W=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $y$. It also contains $x$, since an open containing a specialization contains its generalizations. Let $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q$ represent $x,y$. The spectrum dictionary gives $\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak q$. Step 4, the affine-stalk identification $\mathcal O_{X,x}\cong R_{\mathfrak p}$, and the prime-localization bijection give a chain $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ in $R$: the supremum of the integer chain lengths in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is two, so length two is attained, and a chain of length two must end at its unique maximal ideal. Appending $\mathfrak q$ contradicts $\dim R\leq2$ from Step 3. Thus the closure of $\{x\}$ has no point other than $x$.

source.place: The codimension-two normal-surface observation in Tag 0BGP (theorem-resolve), expanded using prime chains; algebra.tex Tag 00E3 (lemma-spec-localization).

proof.text: The scheme $X$ is Noetherian by hypothesis; $Z$ is closed by Step 2, and all its points are closed in $X$ by Step 5. The closed-point finiteness lemma therefore makes $Z$ finite. Its empty-set case is included.

source.place: Tag 0BA8 (lemma-Noetherian-irreducible-components), closed-point finiteness consequence stated by the cited node.

proof.text: Fix $x\in Z$ and set $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. It is a Noetherian normal local domain by Step 1 and normality of $X$, and has dimension two by Step 4. Take $U_i$ containing $x$. The localization-excellence theorem applied to the excellent ring $R_i$, its identity finite type algebra, and $R_i\setminus\mathfrak p_x$ gives excellence of $A=(R_i)_{\mathfrak p_x}$. Each prime localization of the normal domain $A$ is again a normal domain by localization-normality; in particular $A$ is a normal ring, as needed for the normal-ascent theorem below.

Put $B=\widehat A=\varprojlim_n A/\mathfrak m^n$. Completion-Noetherianity makes $B$ Noetherian. The local-completion theorem makes it local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mB$. Since $A$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated, so the completion-mod-ideal theorem makes $B$ complete for $\mathfrak mB$, precisely its maximal-ideal topology. Finally completion-dimension gives $\dim B=\dim A=2$.

Excellence of $A$ includes the G-ring property. Apply G-ring completion-regularity to the ideal $\mathfrak m$: $A\to B$ is flat, and every fibre $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is Noetherian and geometrically regular. Taking the trivial finite purely inseparable extension in the definition of geometric regularity makes each fibre a regular ring. Regular-implies-normal makes every fibre normal. The flat normal-fibre ascent theorem now applies: both $A$ and $B$ are Noetherian, $A$ is a normal ring by Step 7, the completion map is flat, and its fibres are normal. It follows that $B$ is a normal ring.

source.place: Tag 0C23 (lemma-completion-normal-local-ring), expanded through Tag 0AH2 (lemma-map-G-ring-to-completion-regular), algebra.tex Tags 0567 (lemma-regular-normal) and 0C22 (lemma-normal-goes-up-noetherian).

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak mB$ be the unique maximal ideal of $B$. By the definition of normal ring, $B_{\mathfrak n}$ is a normal domain. Since every denominator outside $\mathfrak n$ is already a unit in the local ring $B$, the maps $B\to B_{\mathfrak n}$ and $b/s\mapsto bs^{-1}$ are inverse ring isomorphisms. Thus $B$ itself is a normal domain. Combined with Step 8, this is the required complete Noetherian normal local domain of dimension two.

source.place: Conclusion of Tag 0C23 (lemma-completion-normal-local-ring), using normality at the maximal ideal of a local ring.
